Import Libraries

Six libraries covering data manipulation, visualisation, statistical modelling, and machine learning.

Load Data

Read AEP_hourly.csv, parse Datetime as index, sort chronologically, inspect shape and missing values.

Step 3

Exploratory Data Analysis

Break down average consumption by hour of day, day of week, and month to reveal the seasonal structure hidden in the raw signal.

Average MW by Hour / Day of Week / Month
Left: peak around midday. Centre: weekdays ~1,100 MW above weekends. Right: Jan & Jul peaks from heating/cooling demand.
Step 4

Stationarity Check & Decomposition

The Augmented Dickey-Fuller test checks whether the series has a unit root (non-stationary). Then seasonal decomposition splits the signal into four components.

ADF Statistic : -18.2859 p-value : 0.0 Stationary : Yes ✓ (p < 0.05 → reject unit root hypothesis)
Seasonal Decomposition (additive model, period = 7 days)
Top to bottom: observed signal, long-term trend, weekly seasonal pattern, and residual noise. The trend shows a mild dip around 2009–2012.
Step 5

Feature Engineering & Train / Test Split

Resample to daily averages, then create 8 predictive features. Split 80 / 20 with shuffle=False to preserve time order.

X_train shape : (4020, 8) X_test shape : (1005, 8) Train period : 2004-10-31 → 2015-11-02 Test period : 2015-11-03 → 2018-08-03 Features : dayofweek, month, dayofyear, lag_1, lag_7, lag_14, rolling_7, rolling_30
Step 6

Model 1 — SARIMA

SARIMAX(1,0,1)(1,1,1)[7] trained on the raw daily target series. Forecasts the held-out test window in a single batch.

SARIMA Statistical

Seasonal AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average. Works directly on the target series — no engineered features needed. The seasonal order (1,1,1)[7] handles the weekly cycle.

  • order=(1,0,1) — AR(1), no differencing, MA(1)
  • seasonal_order=(1,1,1)[7] — weekly seasonality
  • enforce_stationarity=False, enforce_invertibility=False
SARIMA Forecast vs Actual — Test Period (Nov 2015 → Aug 2018)
SARIMA captures the early weeks but drifts to a fixed seasonal mean as the forecast horizon extends — a known limitation of ARIMA on long horizons.
Step 7

Model 2 — XGBoost

200 gradient-boosted trees trained on all 8 engineered features. Learns non-linear relationships between lag values, rolling averages, and calendar patterns.

XGBoost ML Model

Gradient-boosted decision trees. Exploits lag and rolling features that capture both short-term autocorrelation and medium-term trends.

  • n_estimators=200, learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=5
  • random_state=42 for reproducibility
  • Predicts each test day independently using its features
XGBoost Forecast vs Actual — Test Period (Nov 2015 → Aug 2018)
XGBoost tracks the actual signal closely throughout the full 2.7-year test window, including seasonal peaks and weekly oscillations.

Forecast Comparison

SARIMA (top) vs XGBoost (bottom) — Same Test Window

Takeaways

Key Insights

What the notebook results tell us about the data and the models.

✅

Confirmed Stationary

ADF statistic −18.29, p-value = 0.0. Far below threshold — series is stable over time.

🕛

Daily Peak ~Midday

EDA shows consumption peaks 11AM–3PM and drops to a trough between midnight–5AM.

📆

Weekend Dip

Mon–Fri significantly higher than Sat–Sun, reflecting industrial & commercial demand.

❄️🌞

Jan & Jul Peaks

Winter heating and summer cooling drive the two annual demand peaks in the monthly chart.

📉

SARIMA Drifts

MAE 1,465 MW. Accurate for ~2 months then converges to a fixed seasonal mean — horizon problem.

🚀

XGBoost: 60% Better

MAE 597 MW, MAPE 4.08%. Lag features keep the model anchored to recent actual values throughout.
